title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 217: The Vanishing Vault: Light Pollution
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 217 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Vanishing Vault: Light Pollution and the Architecture of Darkness

Paragraph 1. Throughout almost all of human history, the night sky served as a natural guide. Ancient communities watched star patterns to tell stories, plan seasonal farming calendars, and sail safely across oceans. Over the last century, however, the rapid growth of outdoor artificial lighting has broken this connection. According to international surveys, over eighty percent of humans globally—and ninety-nine percent of residents in the United States and Europe—live beneath skies polluted by artificial glow. In modern cities, true night has disappeared behind a permanent yellow twilight.

Paragraph 2. Urban skyglow is mainly caused by poor lamp design. Instead of shining only onto pavements where walkers need safety, conventional streetlights and glowing billboards send large amounts of light sideways or upward. Once these light rays enter the lower air, they bounce off gas molecules, tiny drops of moisture, and dust particles—a process called Rayleigh scattering. This scattered light bounces back down like a glowing roof, hiding faint stars so that only the Moon and brightest planets stay visible.

Paragraph 3. Constant night brightness creates serious harm across nature. Insects that normally steer by starlight fly endlessly around roadside bulbs until they collapse or get caught by bats. Along beaches, baby sea turtles are programmed to crawl toward the bright moonlit sea; instead, bright resort lights draw them inland toward dry sand and cars. In humans, blue light from street lamps and digital screens lowers nighttime melatonin, a hormone needed for deep rest, increasing risks of heart trouble.

Paragraph 4. To fight light pollution, engineers and city planners are promoting smarter lighting rules. Importantly, cities do not need to switch off all public lights. Instead, workers install shielded fixtures that point light strictly downward onto streets, and swap harsh blue-white LEDs for warm-coloured bulbs. In northern Chile and the Canary Islands, dark-sky ordinances near telescopes improved night clarity while cutting municipal energy bills by over thirty percent.

Paragraph 5. Conservation groups are also protecting natural darkness as a shared human treasure. The International Dark-Sky Association has named over two hundred protected reserves globally, including parks in New Zealand and Namibia. Protecting dark skies is not only helpful for professional astronomers; it allows ordinary citizens to enjoy the same starry universe that inspired human art and science for millennia.
